effect_estimate.comment: All exact numbers are extracted directly from the readable body text and footnotes (back-matter table pages PDF pp. 39-46, 48, and 50 were embedded as non-text images in the PDF).
effect_estimate.value: Strategic water under-servicing (1991 share of 1-3 room houses with central water connection, urban area FE): inverse-density-weighted neighbor servicing slope beta = -0.43 (lagged-covariate OLS) and -0.53 (spatial MLE; -0.69 OLS and -0.59 MLE with equal weights), implying a 1 percentage point increase in neighboring localities' small-house water servicing reduces own-locality small-house water servicing by ~0.45 percentage points; moving from lowest to highest locality income and size quintiles raises small-house water servicing by 0.48 (48 percentage points) before interaction, but the negative top-quintile income x size interaction reduces that increase by 0.16 (16 percentage points), and in the 2-3 locality urban area subsample marginal income and size effects turn negative at >=0.5 SD above mean size and >=1 SD above mean income; strategic and wealth-size under-servicing effects disappear for large houses in 1991 and for small houses by 2000 after post-1988 democratization and slum-upgrading reforms. Descriptive disparities: in 1980, 61% of small houses (1-2 rooms) vs. 86% of large houses (6-7 rooms) had central water connections, and 17% vs. 54% had full service (water, sewer, electricity); in 1991, ~14% of urban households lacked central water and ~51% lacked full service; localities with municipal minimum lot-size zoning >125 sq m had higher ratios of untitled-to-titled homeowners and migrants-to-non-migrants in 2000. IV growth impact (1991-2000 locality household growth, urban area FE): 2SLS beta = 0.74 (0.77 with shorter instrument list; 0.78 with river/altitude instruments; p < 0.10, first-stage partial F ~ 13; LIML p ~ 0.05), where for a ~0.8 point estimate a 1 SD (0.21) reduction in 1991 small-house water servicing reduces 1991-2000 total household growth (mean 0.40) and low-educated household growth by 0.17 (17 percentage points), with a similar positive IV effect on higher-educated households; using share of untitled homes with central water yields OLS = -0.16 and LIML = 1.82 (SE = 2.22, partial F = 6.2). 1980 district-FE rent hedonics: central water connection commands a 12% rent premium in Sao Paulo and 23% in Rio de Janeiro, and central sewer commands 9% and 18% over no connection.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 1 (documented association): the water-servicing determinant regressions (Section 4) rely on observational lagged-covariate OLS and spatial MLE without valid instruments (the authors note instruments for neighbor servicing were unacceptably weak), and exclusionary municipal policy is proxied indirectly via census water connection rates for small (1-3 room) houses rather than direct administrative observation of utility refusals or legal enforcement (and the IV in Section 5 estimates downstream population growth with borderline significance p < 0.10 and partial F ~ 13 across multiple endogenous regressors, corresponding to Serious ROBINS-I risk of bias).
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 6, Section 1; PDF pp. 10-14, Sections 2.3-2.5; PDF pp. 21-28, Section 4; PDF pp. 31-33, Section 5.1-5.2

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines informal housing tenure (favelas and loteamentos lacking land title) and pre-1988 legal prohibitions on municipal water/sewer provision to informal settlements, formal land ownership/title status, national (125 sq m) and stricter municipal minimum lot-size zoning laws, strategic municipal infrastructure planning and discretion to withhold water connections from small-house neighborhoods, metropolitan jurisdictional fragmentation across municipalities/state vs. local utilities, and inter-municipal strategic interaction plus electoral/democratization politics.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Non-randomized panel/quasi-experimental econometric study using urban area fixed effects, lagged covariates/spatial MLE for strategic policy choice (Section 4), and 2SLS/LIML instrumental variables (geology/insolation and 1970 historical instruments) for causal effects of municipal water under-servicing on locality growth (Section 5).

study_design.comment: Combines a game-theoretic spatial equilibrium model of inter-locality migration and public service provision with multi-decade municipal panel/cross-sectional regressions, spatial econometrics, and instrumental variables estimation.
study_design.value: Theoretical spatial-equilibrium model with longitudinal/panel and quasi-experimental econometric analysis of census and municipal data (1970-2000): urban-area fixed-effects OLS and spatial MLE strategic-interaction regressions (1980-1991), 2SLS/LIML instrumental-variables locality growth regressions (1991-2000), and district-fixed-effects hedonic rent regressions (1980)
study_design.where_found: PDF pp. 7-8, Section 2.1; PDF pp. 14-23, Sections 3-4; PDF pp. 28-32, Section 5; PDF p. 47, Appendix A

evidence_quotes.quote: Richer and larger localities in an urban area reduce provision of water and sewerage connections to the smaller houses in which poorer migrants would live to discourage the in-migration of these poorer migrants and deflect them to other localities.
for localities to provide public infrastructure such as central sewer and water connections in either type of settlement. This gave an opportunistic excuse to deny or limit such provision.
The 123 urban areas are composed of 447 localities (MCAs), which in 1991, consisted of 659 municipalities.
In 1980, only 61% of small houses in our localities had a water connection while 86% of large houses had a water connection.

For a point estimate of 0.8, a one standard deviation (0.21) increase in servicing leads to an increase of 0.17 (for which the mean is 0.40) in the growth rate in the number of households during the decade.
